lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: It's nice to meet you, neighbor. My name is Ed. I work at the Grain Elevator here in Longview, over by the Train Depot. After you harvest your grain, bring it to me. I'll buy your grain and store it in the Grain Elevator until someone in Kansas City buys it.

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.text: They call me Ma Watson. 25 years ago, I came here from Chicago with my dear husband. We built a sod house right away. Your neighbors will help you build a sod in no time at all.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: My name is Norman. I was born right here, back in the wild days before Kansas was a state. I work in the bank. If someone from out of town sends you money, you can come to me to collect it.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: Hello, I'm Harriet. When I was a little girl, my family moved here from Ohio. When you need to buy things for your farm, like seeds or a ready-made windmill, you can come to my general store. If you need to buy a horse or another animal, you should go to the livestock fair. Every April and May, folks trade all kinds of farm animals there.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: My name is Sven. I'm your nearest neighbor. My family and I came here from Sweden seven years ago. We started farming a homestead. If you don't dig a well soon, you'll lose your homestead claim. You'll have to dig deep because the water is deep below the surface. You should build a windmill to pump the water up to the surface.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Howdy! My name is Daniel. You'll need a proper house to survive the Kansas winter. Soon some other neighbors and I will help you build a sod house. Then you'll need to plant a few acres of spring wheat.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: Neighbor, how are you? I'm Sophie. My husband and I run a big cattle ranch just west of here. These are my two children, Kate and Jesse.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.text: My name's Kate. I wish I didn't have to sit here next to my brother Jesse. He's such a pest!

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I'm Jesse, and I'd rather be playing in the field than sitting next to my boring sister Kate.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Hi there, neighbor. Remember to bring me your crops when you harvest them. I'll store them in the grain elevator. If you come early in the season, I'll give you my best price!

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.text: What a beautiful fall day. It's harvest time.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: How are you, neighbor? I hope you'll be a successful homesteader. If you need more money to buy equipment or seeds, you can apply for a loan from the bank.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: Hi, neighbor. How's life on the homestead? Come by the general store and take a look at our mail order catalog. I always keep the newest catalog handy. Sometimes there are new products for sale.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Do you know how to tell if your wheat is ready to harvest, neighbor? Wait three days once you think it's ready. Then, taste one kernel of wheat. If the kernel's hard, then the wheat is ready to harvest. If you want, you can read my newspaper. There's an article about new ways to grow wheat. Would you like to read it?

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: It's finally harvest time. We usually help each other with the harvest because it's important to harvest wheat as soon as it's ready. Otherwise it'll go bad. Sometimes you can help us and we'll be glad to help you.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: Hi neighbour, we ranchers like to grow food too. Now it's time to start canning vegetables from my garden. We'll have enough canned peas and beans for the whole winter.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.text: When I'm bigger, Ma will let me help her bake bread [?].

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I'd rather go fishing in the creek. You can come, Katie, if you try to catch some fish too.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Hi there, neighbor! If you planted winter wheat, be sure to come to see me once you've finished harvesting!

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.text: Do you know how to figure out how much wheat you've grown? If you throw a hat into a wheat field, the number of heads of wheat under the hat is the number of bushels of wheat you'll harvest per acre.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: Sven, I hear that you farmers are putting up a fuss about the price of wheat these days. I don't understand why. I hear that in Chicago the price of wheat is $1.20 per bushel. That sounds fair to me.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. How's your baby boy? When you're not busy with the harvest, please bring him by for a visit.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Yeah, but the farmer does not receive $1.20 per bushel. The grain elevator operator in the small town pays the farmer much less. The railroad companies which own the grain elevators make all the profits.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Hi there, neighbor. Remember to harvest as quickly as you can. You'll get a better price for your grain, and you'll have time to plant some spring wheat.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: Hello neighbor. Say, did you see how quickly they're building this new schoolhouse? I'm sure it will be ready for the full term.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.text: Aww.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Aww!

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Hi there, neighbor!

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.text: [snoring]

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: I'm glad I'm not a farmer. I don't have to work hard all day long to get the harvest in on time. Once you're done, you have to start plowing right away so you can plant winter wheat.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. I saw your little girl the other day. She's as cute as a pumpkin, and she's growing quickly, too. If you need something for her, I can order it at the general store.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Yeah Norman, you work hard, but it's fun, we eat lots of great food at harvest time, including my wife's pies and cakes as big as Texas. Also, it's good to work outside with your neighbors. I wouldn't want to sit inside a bank every day like you.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Hi there, neighbor. Here's some friendly advice. Last year, they passed a new law in Kansas. Now it's illegal to make or sell liquor in our state. Some folks disagree and are trying to sell moonshine. I'd keep away from that business if I were you.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: Be careful Ed, you lose your balance, don't you know it's bad luck to tip your chair back?

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.text: Hush, Jesse. Children should be seen and not heard.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Ma, what's moonshine?

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Hi there, neighbor. I see you're still working on your homestead claim. Did you know that you farmers are actually changing the weather in the Great Plains? Some folks say that rain follows the plough.

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.text: Ed, that's the silliest idea I've ever heard. I've lived in Kansas for many years. Believe me, plowing the land does not bring more rain. We're just going through a wet spell for a few years. One of these years we'll have a dry spell, and then you'll see that I'm right.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: How are you, neighbor? You have three more years to work your homestead, and then the land's yours, free and clear.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. I heard your little girl was sick. I hope she's better now. Folks around here admire you, homesteaders. Somehow you managed to take good care of your families. It must be very difficult.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Yeah Norman, free and clear, but a farmer who owes the bank lots of money is not free and clear until the loan is repaid. Everyone makes a profit from the little farmer.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: I suppose it's harvest time.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: We just sold some beautiful heifers at the Livestock Fair. Feel free to stop by and check them out if you're in the market for a dairy cow.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.text: Hush, Jesse. Children should be seen and not heard.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: MMMMMMMM

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Hi there, neighbour. Be sure to come and see me after the harvest. My grain elevator is the only one in town.

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.text: Are you going to plant winter wheat, neighbor? Remember what the old-timers say. Plant your crop by the light of the new moon, because land that's plowed at that time will not get hard, and you'll have a good crop.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: I'd like to see that, Sven. You have your farmers' alliances, but until you have votes in Congress, you have no power against the railroads. You're just like wheat blowing in the wind.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: Hello neighbor, it's nice to see you again.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Yeah, and that's the problem, I say. You have no competition, so you'll pay us whatever you want. Someday we farmers will get together and build our own grain elevators. Then we'll get a fair price for our crops.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: I don't have much to say today.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: Children now that summer is over you can go to school. I'll miss your help at home. There is always so much to do

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.text: Yes, there's washing clothes, baking bread, taking care of the chickens, canning fruit and vegetables, and keeping the prairie dust out of our house.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I think my chores should be riding the horses so they don't get lonely.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: That's true, but you take a big risk sending your precious crops all the way to O'Grady. But that's a full day's drive. On the way, a sudden storm could ruin your grain. It's much safer to bring your crops to the grain elevator in good old Longview.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Hello neighbor, have you heard? There's another way to sell your crops. Sometimes a fellow shows up here on Main Street. You can pay him to take your crops to the town of O'Grady, just 10 miles north of here. A different railway comes into O'Grady and the grain elevator there sometimes offers a better price.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: I'll sell my crops to the grain elevator that pays the best price, after I take shipping prices into account.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Hi there, neighbour. You farmers are finally getting what you wanted! Prices for wheat are rising!

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.text: Do you remember when I predicted there'd be another dry spell? Well, I think it started. Even though we had another terrible winter, I bet this summer will be dry again. You can read about the drought in Sven's paper.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: You farmers must be happy about the law to regulate commerce that Congress passed. I just read about it in the newspaper.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: Hello neighbor, did you read about the new steam engine tractors? You can order one through the catalog at my store.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Yeah, but that's because of the dry summer we had last year. There is less wheat for sale this year, so the price is higher.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Everyone is wondering if a drought is starting. If it is, I'm not going to plant all my land. There's no point in wasting good seed.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: The winter was terrible, especially for us ranchers. So many of our cattle died in the blizzards. Some of the cattle just froze where they stood. Some ranchers are giving up and leaving for other states. They're selling their land to farmers. But we've decided to stay.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.text: During the terrible January blizzard, my brother Jesse nearly lost his way between the house and the barn.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I went to look for the cows, and then everything disappeared in a cloud of snow. It's hard to find white cows in a blizzard.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Hi there, neighbor. If you planted a crop last spring, I hope you have a good harvest.

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.text: It seems that I was right. There's a real drought here. I hope it ends soon, or we'll see lots of homesteaders packing up their wagons and going back east.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: Ma Watson, when you're right, you're right.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: Sophie, I heard that your brother is coming back to Kansas.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Yeah, and all of you are right, all right. But I wish you were wrong. We need rain.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: You sure are right Norman, you're right that she's right.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: Yes he is. He used to work for a labor union in Chicago. After the Haymarket riot last year he decided to find a quieter line of work. I think he wants to sell steam engine tractors.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.text: If I could go to New York, I'd rather see the Statue of Liberty that France gave us last year. If I wanted to ride the train up a mountain, I'd go to the Rockies in Colorado.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I wanna go to New York, to a place called Coney Island. There's a train there called a roller coaster. It goes up and down a steep mountain very quickly.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Sven, I read in your newspaper that President Cleveland wants to get rid of the tax on products from overseas.

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.text: Hi, neighbor. How are you? I see your oldest daughter is growing into a fine young lady. If she gets a good education, she could go far. These days, a woman can do all sorts of jobs. Just ask Sophie about her sister-in-law, Mary Lohman.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: Harriet, I read in Sven's paper that the Kodak company is selling a great new camera. Can I order it through your store?

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: You sure can, Norman. Just look in the catalog. The camera will be delivered to you within two weeks, and then you can start taking your own pictures. You'll just love being able to fill up your own picture albums.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Yeah, and this is not good. It is not fair that people in America can buy things from other countries so cheaply. Then they will not buy American products. The tax is good, because it makes products from other countries more expensive.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: It seems that the drought will last for at least another year. I wonder when we'll have a normal rainy season.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: Did you hear about my sister-in-law Mary Lohmann? She was just elected mayor of Oskaloosa, Kansas. Five other women were elected to the city council. Do you know that Oskaloosa has the first all-female city government in America? We certainly are living in historic times.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.text: When I grow up, I want to be either Mayor of Longview or President of the United States. I know that I don't want to live on a farm. It's too much work.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I want to be a cowboy or a rancher or maybe a lawyer.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: That's true, but you take a big risk sending your precious crops all the way to O'Grady. That's a full day's drive. On the way, a sudden storm could ruin your grain. It's much safer to bring your crops to the grain elevator in good old Longview.

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.text: Hi, neighbor. How are you? I heard that a lot of folks in the Farmer's Alliance are starting to put up a fuss. They're angry at the railroad companies, which also own the grain elevators. I'm sure that many farmers around here would love to start their own political party.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: Hi, neighbor. I'm glad to see you're sticking it out here in Kansas. Some farmers couldn't repay their loans, and the bank took away their farms. Other farmers are doing so well that they're buying new steam engine tractors. You can order one now in the catalog in the general store.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: Sophie, have you heard about the new literary society? Every Friday night there's some kind of show at the town hall.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Hello neighbor. Have you heard? There's another way to sell your crops. Sometimes a fellow shows up here on Main Street. You can pay him to take your crops to the town of O'Grady just 10 miles north of here. A different railway comes into O'Grady and the grain elevator there sometimes offers a better price.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: I'll sell my crops to the grain elevator that pays the best price after I take shipping prices into account.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: I went last week Harriet, it was so much fun. First there was a big spelling bee and then music and dancing.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.text: I had a nice time at the social last Friday night, didn't you Jesse?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I was too busy making sure that [pesky?] Billy Guthrie didn't dance with you too much. I think he's sweet on you. He'd better watch out, sis. Those Dodge City boys are wild and dangerous.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.context: Town talk 111 — Sep 17, 1893 (Cherokee Strip land run)
lines.text: Hello neighbor. I hope you'll bring your crops to me instead of sending them to O'Grady. In these hard times, you can't take the chance of losing your crop.

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.context: Town talk 111 — Sep 17, 1893 (Cherokee Strip land run)
lines.text: Hi, neighbor. Have you heard about the second big land rush in Oklahoma? Folks built a new town in just a few days. We may be going through hard times right now, but the pioneer spirit is still alive.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.context: Town talk 111 — Sep 17, 1893 (Cherokee Strip land run)
lines.text: How are you, neighbor?

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.context: Town talk 111 — Sep 17, 1893 (Cherokee Strip land run)
lines.text: It's nice to see you, neighbor. I've heard that your daughter and her husband are very happy together. I'm so glad for them. I hope they'll find work in Longview or nearby.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.context: Town talk 111 — Sep 17, 1893 (Cherokee Strip land run)
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. I just read in my newspaper about how the economic depression is affecting our country. Of course, we farmers already know about that. Prices for our crops have dropped very low.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.context: Town talk 111 — Sep 17, 1893 (Cherokee Strip land run)
lines.text: Howdy, neighbor. Have you read in the paper about how the railroad companies are still stealing from the farmers? I'm voting for the populist party. They'll fight to help the farmers.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.context: Town talk 111 — Sep 17, 1893 (Cherokee Strip land run)
lines.text: Last week I heard a speech by a Kansas woman named Mary Lease. She said that the farmer should raise less corn and more hell. She yelled a lot and now they call her Mary Yellin' Lease.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.context: Town talk 111 — Sep 17, 1893 (Cherokee Strip land run)
lines.text: Hi, guess what? I'm buying a sewing machine through this year's catalog. Then I can sew my own wedding dress. I'm getting married next month to Billy Guthrie.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.context: Town talk 111 — Sep 17, 1893 (Cherokee Strip land run)
lines.text: I'm glad that you're going to the Columbian Exposition in Chicago for your honeymoon. But then you and Billy are moving to Kansas City. That's so far away.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Hello, neighbour. My grain elevator's still full because no trains have come by to unload it. I can't buy any grain until the strike ends!

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.text: Hi, neighbor!

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: This railway strike is already a month old. It's bad news for all of us. Our business depends on the railroads. No one knows when or how the strike will end.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: I'm having a hard time getting supplies for my store. Even though the strike is just against the Pullman Company, there are Pullman cars on almost every railway line. The union workers refuse to work on any line with even one Pullman car. As a result, most railway lines aren't moving at all.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. All we farmers are in the same boat. We can't sell our crops until the trains start moving. Still, I support the American Railway Union workers. Look at my newspaper. You can see how unfairly the Pullman Company treated its workers.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Howdy, neighbor. Have you read the newspaper article about the march on Washington? I suppose those folks are fed up and decided to complain to the boss. I mean the president.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: Did you hear what happened on Main Street last night? A woman called Carrie Nation came into the saloon. She smashed all the bottles of liquor with a hatchet. She said that it's illegal to sell alcohol in our state. She's right, but that axe looked pretty dangerous.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Does anybody want to play some basketball? There's nothing to do in this town, except for watching the paint peel on the Longview Hotel.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Hello there, neighbor!

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.text: [snoring]

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: How are you, Harriet? Have you heard that the laundry on Main Street is for sale? I wonder if the owners are leaving because of financial problems.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: It's not easy to run a business these days. Folks say the economy will take a few years to improve. It's smart to buy a business like the laundry now when it's cheap. Later on, it could make lots of money.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: How are you, neighbor? It's about time for us to go to work in our fields, yeah? Some farmers are starting to get involved in business in town. Maybe that's a good idea.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: It's good to see you, neighbor.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: Hello neighbour, do you know that my husband just bought a small store in town? He wants to be on the school board. In order to do so, you have to own a house or other property in town.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Hi, neighbor. Well, you won't be seeing me on the streets of Longview after next month. I'm going to make my way to California. There's nothing for me to do here, and I'm not cut out for college. I'll see you around someday.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: I hope your daughter can go to college, neighbor. If old Ma Watson were still alive, she would have been proud.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: Hi there, neighbor. I've heard that your youngest daughter is applying to college. You country folk sure are moving up in the world.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. I hope your daughter is accepted by the college. Oberlin is a fine school. It's expensive, but I'm sure it's worth it.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: One of my daughters wanted to go to college but I didn't have enough money back then. Sometimes there are things you can't do for your children. You can only try your best.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Education sure is wonderful, isn't it, neighbor? Now even the young ladies want to go away to college. Your daughter is very brave.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: Hello neighbour, I suppose a successful farmer like you doesn't think twice about sending a child to college. We ranchers are the same way.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Take me out to the ball game. Take me out to the field. Buy me some peanuts and cracker jacks. I don't care if we never come back. For it's root, root, root for the home team. If they don't win it's a shame. For it's one, two, three strikes you're out in the old ball game.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: How are you, neighbor? Now that the Enlarged Homestead Act was passed, will you increase the size of your farm? I think any good farmer would be wise to enlarge the homestead.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: If you want to buy a car, you can order one through the catalogue in my store. I read in the newspaper that the Model T is very popular now. If Ma Watson were still around, she'd be amazed at how many people in Longview own automobiles.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. Have you heard the good news? The government passed a bill that lets homesteaders claim twice as much land as before. You can read about it in the newspaper.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: It's good to see you, neighbor. Thanks to the new Enlarged Homestead Act, I can add 160 more acres onto my farm. My two sons want to be farmers too. They will help me work the extra land.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: Hello neighbour, have you seen our new car? It's parked at the end of the road. Going for a drive is very exciting. The only problem is that these roads are so muddy. If the town ever paves the road, all the drivers will be grateful.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Neighbor, have you heard the news? There's a war in Europe! Great Britain has declared war in Germany!

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: I wonder what the war in Europe will do to our economy. We Americans have to look out for ourselves.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: I sure hope we don't get mixed up in the war in Europe. I don't want our young men to fight.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. Everybody's talking about the war in Europe. The newspaper is full of articles about it.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Some folks say the war might be good for us farmers. The farmers in Europe won't be able to work their fields. If the war continues, the Europeans will need to buy our crops.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: If the war in Europe continues, we should help Britain and France. Many of our families come from there. I don't want Germany to invade those countries. I would even send my son to fight against Germany.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: I just heard the news! We're in the war! America has declared war on Germany and its allies!

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: It's about time we started to fight back. How many of our ships could we let the Germans sink? America must look after itself, and that means putting up a fight.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: It's terrible to think about all those people dying in the war. I hope we can beat the Germans soon, so that people will stop dying.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Yeah, war is terrible, but it's also good for us farmers. Our friends in Europe need our grain. They are paying us a good price for it. Now we will send them our grain and our sons. Why shouldn't we get paid?

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: I don't wanna make a profit from the war, my sons are too old to be drafted, but I guess your younger son will be sent Sophie, I hope he comes back safe and sound.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: My son is sure to be drafted. He will be a good soldier and he will bring honor to his country. We are proud to fight for America and for all the free democratic countries in the world.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: I just heard the news! The war is over! The war is over!

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: I'm so happy that the war is finally over. It's been a terrible year. My brother was wounded in France and three of my cousins died of the Spanish flu.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: I hope that our lives will get back to normal soon. In the past year, it's been hard to find coffee and sugar. So many farmers have had trouble finding help in the fields. All the young men are overseas.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: You can be sure that things will be different now. Now our economy is part of the world economy. I wonder how long the Europeans will keep buying so much grain from us at such a high price.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: The Germans say they won't fight anymore. Let's see what happens when they have to sign a peace treaty with all the countries they attacked.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: I'm so happy. My son came through the war safely. Neighbor, I heard that your son was actually a hero over in France. I heard that he saved his whole platoon. We can't wait to see our sons again.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Hi there, neighbor. I have some good news for you, farmers. America is continuing to send grain to Europe. That's good news for me, too!

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: Hi there, neighbor. I have some good news for you farmers. America's continuing to send grain to Europe. That's good news for me too!

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: The 18th Amendment was passed on January 17th. Next January, when it goes into effect, the rest of the country will know what Kansas already knows. Making alcohol illegal doesn't stop people from drinking it.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: Now, Norman, you don't know that the law won't work. Many Americans agree that drinking is bad. That's why the amendment was ratified.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. This is a good time for the farmers. The price of wheat is high. We can use our tractors to grow more and more grain. I think our children and our grandchildren will have good lives in this country.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Howdy, neighbor. Do you remember how many farmers left Kansas back in the 1890s? Aren't you glad that you stayed? This is the best place to live in America.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: I hope the new law works. I also hope that another amendment will be ratified. Folks say that by next year, maybe American women will have the right to vote. It's about time!

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.context: Town talk 120 — Dec 1919 (finale, "Home on the Range")
lines.text: Oh, give me a home, where the buffalo roam, and the deer and the antelope play. Where seldom is heard a discouraging word, and the skies are not cloudy all day. Home, home on the range, where the deer and the antelope play. Where seldom is heard a discouraging word, and the skies are not cloudy all day.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.context: Town talk 120 — Dec 1919 (finale, "Home on the Range")
lines.text: Oh, give me a home where the buffalo roam And the deer and the antelope play Where seldom is heard a discouraging word And the skies are not cloudy all day Home, home on the range Where the deer and the antelope play Where seldom is heard a discouraging word And the skies are not cloudy all day

Home, home on the range, Where the deer and the antelope play, Where seldom is heard a discouraging word, And the skies are not cloudy all day.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.context: Town talk 201 — Jul 1893, daughter's modest wedding
lines.text: Congratulations on your daughter's wedding!

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.context: Town talk 201 — Jul 1893, daughter's modest wedding
lines.text: I wish them well. I wish I could have seen the wedding.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.context: Town talk 201 — Jul 1893, daughter's modest wedding
lines.text: I heard that your daughter got married. I hope they're very happy together.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.context: Town talk 201 — Jul 1893, daughter's modest wedding
lines.text: I heard about your daughter's wedding, I hope it was nice.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.context: Town talk 201 — Jul 1893, daughter's modest wedding
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. I want to congratulate you on your daughter's marriage.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.context: Town talk 201 — Jul 1893, daughter's modest wedding
lines.text: Congratulations, neighbor. I want to wish the young couple many years of happiness.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.context: Town talk 201 — Jul 1893, daughter's modest wedding
lines.text: You must be pleased as punch, neighbor. Congratulations!

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.context: Town talk 201 — Jul 1893, daughter's modest wedding
lines.text: I heard your daughter got married. Congratulations! I hope that I'll get married soon.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.context: Town talk 202 — Jul 1893, daughter's nice wedding
lines.text: Congratulations on your daughter's wedding!

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.context: Town talk 202 — Jul 1893, daughter's nice wedding
lines.text: What a beautiful wedding! It was nice of you to invite me.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.context: Town talk 202 — Jul 1893, daughter's nice wedding
lines.text: I heard that your daughter got married. I hope that they're very happy together.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.context: Town talk 202 — Jul 1893, daughter's nice wedding
lines.text: I really enjoyed the wedding. Please give my best wishes to your whole family.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.context: Town talk 202 — Jul 1893, daughter's nice wedding
lines.text: Hello neighbor! You made a fine wedding for your daughter. You must be doing pretty well for yourself.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.context: Town talk 202 — Jul 1893, daughter's nice wedding
lines.text: Congratulations, neighbor. I want to extend my best wishes to the happy couple.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.context: Town talk 202 — Jul 1893, daughter's nice wedding
lines.text: You must be pleased as punch neighbour. Congratulations!

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.context: Town talk 202 — Jul 1893, daughter's nice wedding
lines.text: I heard your daughter got married. Congratulations! I hope that I'll get married soon.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.context: Town talk 203 — Jul 1893, daughter's grand wedding
lines.text: Neighbour, it was so nice of you to invite the whole town to your daughter's wedding! None of us will ever forget it!

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.context: Town talk 203 — Jul 1893, daughter's grand wedding
lines.text: I've never seen such a beautiful wedding neighbor. Thank you so much for inviting everyone!

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.context: Town talk 203 — Jul 1893, daughter's grand wedding
lines.text: Neighbor you are a fine and generous person that was quite a wedding you made for your daughter

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.context: Town talk 203 — Jul 1893, daughter's grand wedding
lines.text: What a terrific wedding! The town will be talking about it for years to come!

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.context: Town talk 203 — Jul 1893, daughter's grand wedding
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. That was a wonderful wedding you made for your daughter. You must be doing pretty well for yourself.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.context: Town talk 203 — Jul 1893, daughter's grand wedding
lines.text: Howdy neighbor. It sure was nice of you to invite all of us to your daughter's wedding. I'll never forget it.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.context: Town talk 203 — Jul 1893, daughter's grand wedding
lines.text: Neighbour, that was quite a wedding. No one in town will ever forget what a nice thing you did, inviting everybody to the wedding.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.context: Town talk 203 — Jul 1893, daughter's grand wedding
lines.text: I just loved your daughter's wedding. When I get married, we're going to invite your family.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.context: Town talk 204 — Jul 1902, son's modest wedding
lines.text: Congratulations on your son's wedding.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.context: Town talk 220 — Sep, cattle trampled unfenced fields
lines.text: Hi, neighbor. I heard that some cattle got into your fields. Folks say that some day there won't be any herds of range cattle left around here. Every year there are fewer, but you still have to watch out for them.

lines.speaker: Ma Watson
lines.context: Town talk 220 — Sep, cattle trampled unfenced fields
lines.text: I remember many years ago when all these farms were just open grasslands. We had Kansa Indians here back then. There were no fences for miles and miles.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.context: Town talk 220 — Sep, cattle trampled unfenced fields
lines.text: Hello neighbor, it's too bad about those cattle. I hear that the ranchers and farmers often fight about who gets the open land, and sometimes the ranchers break down the farmer's fences. Hmm, country folk.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.context: Town talk 220 — Sep, cattle trampled unfenced fields
lines.text: Farmers everywhere are trying to keep cattle out of their fields by putting up fences. The best kind of fence is a barbed wire fence, but there isn't any in Longview yet.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.context: Town talk 220 — Sep, cattle trampled unfenced fields
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. I am sorry to hear about those cattle. I have had that problem many times. Today there are fewer cattle, but when a herd wants to go somewhere, it is very hard to stop it.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.context: Town talk 220 — Sep, cattle trampled unfenced fields
lines.text: I heard a story about a herd of cattle that found a little wooden house on the prairie. They started to brush up against it to scratch their hides. Next thing you know, they pushed that house all the way down the road.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.context: Town talk 220 — Sep, cattle trampled unfenced fields
lines.text: Neighbor, I hope you know that our cattle didn't break into your fields. We keep a close watch on them. The cattle must have belonged to Dan Collins' herd. He doesn't take good care of them. And they wander off looking for water.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.context: Town talk 220 — Sep, cattle trampled unfenced fields
lines.text: One time a herd of cattle surrounded me in a field, luckily I jumped up on a rock and stayed there until they passed, otherwise they would have walked right over me.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.context: Town talk 220 — Sep, cattle trampled unfenced fields
lines.text: I'm not afraid of cows. I go out with our cowboys all the time to watch the herds. I think the cows might be afraid of me.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.context: Town talk 301 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went well
lines.text: Good day to ya!

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.context: Town talk 301 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went well
lines.text: For a country farmer, you're doing a pretty good job as mayor.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.context: Town talk 301 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went well
lines.text: I think you're doing a wonderful job. Keep up the good work!

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.context: Town talk 301 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went well
lines.text: Yeah, I would vote for you again. Good work!

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.context: Town talk 301 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went well
lines.text: Hey, it's the mayor!

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.context: Town talk 301 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went well
lines.text: Hello, how are you?

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.context: Town talk 302 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went badly
lines.text: A good mayor should do what the people want. I'm sure you'll learn eventually.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.context: Town talk 302 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went badly
lines.text: Here's the Mayor of Longview, folks!

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.context: Town talk 302 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went badly
lines.text: That's right. When I think about how you spent our city budget, I wonder if you know what the folks in Longview want. Still, what can we expect from a farmer?

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.context: Town talk 302 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went badly
lines.text: How are you?

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.context: Town talk 302 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went badly
lines.text: Hello there.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.context: Town talk 302 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went badly
lines.text: We're still with you. I'm sure you'll figure out what's best for our town. Keep trying!

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.context: Town talk 302 — Mar 1916–19, mayor's budget went badly
lines.text: I think you're doing a good job, but lots of folks in town aren't sure that you know what they need.

lines.speaker: Ed
lines.text: I have good news, neighbor. Now that we're sending so much grain to Europe, you'll be getting more money for your grain. I'm happy about the extra business, but I'm worried that soon we'll be fighting too.

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: Me too!

lines.speaker: Norman
lines.text: Neighbor, I hear that all you farmers still want the government to control the railroads. Of course, you're more than just a farmer now. Good luck in the race for mayor!

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: No Sven, that's too harsh. Maybe Jack should be fined. But most folks agree with me that jail is not necessary.

lines.speaker: Harriet
lines.text: Three years ago, Kansas gave women the right to vote. I believe all American women deserve that right. I'm sure that most women would vote to make alcohol against the law throughout the country.

lines.speaker: Sven
lines.text: Hello, neighbor. Did you hear that Donnelly's cattle went crazy a few days ago and tore up some of my fields? Those cattle nearly killed my son. If you become mayor, I want you to put that Jack Donnelly behind bars.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: I remember when the ranchers and the farmers used to fight it out with pistols. If you are elected, I hope that you'll make laws to stop the young ones from walking around town with guns. It's too easy for them to get riled up and start shooting.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: I think that a lot of fighting and shooting happens when people are drunk. We have laws against making and selling liquor in Kansas. But too many people break the law. If you are elected, I hope you make sure that the town of Longview stays dry.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: America, the 1880s. Hundreds of thousands of people from around the world have moved to the big cities of the Northeast. You are among them. You have come to pursue the American dream of freedom and prosperity. But your dream has not yet come true. You cannot find a job. Other new Americans work long hours for low pay in steel mills, factories and coal mines. On a cold February day, you wander the streets looking for work. Suddenly something catches your eye that will change your life forever. Come to Kansas where the land is free, where the water is pure, where every farmer is prosperous and as independent as a king. Ride the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe line to Kansas and raise your family in paradise. You take a chance and decide to board a train going west. Your family, husband, wife and five-year-old daughter is on its way to a new life. Railroad lines stretched across the country to connect east and west. Isolated settlements of the Great Plains were finally linked to the rest of the country. People flocked to the area to take advantage of new opportunities in agriculture, industry and trade. Along the way, you stop in the cities that are growing along the railroad lines, canals and rivers. In St. Louis, Kansas City, you meet people who tell you about the paradise that awaits you in a place called Kansas. The soil is so rich that the wheat just grows by itself. I know people who became rich there overnight. You look at the faces of the other immigrants and wonder what their dreams were when they came to America. You think about what their goals are now.
